qs.stem: यदि f, [a,b] पर सतत है, तो f है:-
qs.sol: बंद परिबद्ध अंतराल [a,b] पर सततता से वहाँ रीमान समाकलनीयता मिलती है।
qs.rel: Concept: continuity on a closed bounded interval implies Riemann integrability. Next: it need not be monotone or differentiable; extreme value theorem; fundamental theorem of calculus.

qs.stem: दिया गया समुच्चय U ∈ {(x, y) ∈R²: y > 0, x/y >7} है -
qs.sol: y>0 और x/y>7, y>0 क्षेत्र पर सतत फलनों की सख्त असमानताएँ हैं। उनका प्रतिच्छेद खुला है।
qs.rel: Concept: {y > 0, x/y > 7} is open as an intersection of strict inequalities of continuous functions. Next: closed sets contain limit points; interior and closure; connectedness of the set.

qs.stem: यदि f(x)=1/q किसी परिमेय संख्या x और 0 के लिए अन्यथा, तो निम्न समाकलन ज्ञात करें ?
qs.sol: प्रत्येक अपरिमेय बिंदु पर फलन शून्य है, इसलिए हर निम्न डार्बू योग शून्य है।
qs.rel: Concept: Thomae's function is integrable with integral 0. Next: continuous at irrationals, discontinuous at rationals; Dirichlet function not integrable; lower sums are all 0.

qs.stem: C[a,b] यानी a से b तक सभी निरंतर फलन का समुच्चय जो वास्तविक मान ______ फलन का उपसमुच्चय है?
qs.sol: बंद परिबद्ध अंतराल [a,b] पर सतत वास्तविक मान वाला फलन परिबद्ध होता है।
qs.rel: Concept: a continuous function on [a,b] is bounded. Next: it also attains its maximum and minimum; C[a,b] with sup metric is complete; uniform continuity on compact sets.

qs.stem: एक फलन को ओवर [a,b] s.t. का रीमान समाकलनीय कहा जाता है। ε>0 s.t. के लिए L(f,P) और U(f,P) के बीच स्थित कोई भी संख्या L है?
qs.sol: समाकलनीयता में ऊपरी और निचले योग दोनों एक ही L के मनचाहे निकट आते हैं।
qs.rel: Concept: Riemann integral L is trapped between lower and upper Darboux sums. Next: epsilon-partition criterion U - L < epsilon; refinement; limit of Riemann sums as mesh goes to 0.

qs.stem: फलन f:[a,b]-->R, P और Q [a,b] के विभाजन हैं। P, Q में समाहित है तो?

opts.C: एक सत्य है दूसरा असत्य है

qs.sol: विभाजन के परिष्करण से निचला डार्बू योग घट नहीं सकता।
qs.rel: Concept: refining a partition increases lower sums: L(f,P) <= L(f,Q) and U(f,Q) <= U(f,P). Next: every lower sum <= every upper sum; upper integral = inf U, lower integral = sup L.

qs.stem: किस स्थिति में अनुचित समाकलन, रीमान समाकलन के बराबर हो जाता है?

opts.A: लेबेग समाकलन के एक विशेष स्थिति के रुप में

qs.sol: पूर्वावलोकन कुंजी “लेबेग समाकलन के एक विशेष स्थिति के रूप में” को श्रेय देती है। निरपेक्षतः अभिसारी अनुचित रीमान समाकल उसी लेबेग समाकल के बराबर होता है, पर हर अनुचित समाकल पूरे अंतराल पर रीमान समाकलनीय नहीं होता। मुद्रित तुलना अस्पष्ट है; श्रेय प्राप्त कथन को इस योग्यता के साथ पढ़ना होगा।
qs.rel: Concept: absolutely convergent improper Riemann integral equals the Lebesgue integral. Next: conditionally convergent sin x/x is not Lebesgue integrable; Type I and II improper integrals.

qs.stem: गलत कथन का चयन करें?

opts.A: द्वितीय प्रकार के अनुचित समाकलन में उच्च सीमा पर असातत्य होती है
opts.B: द्वितीय प्रकार के अनुचित समाकलन में निम्न सीमा पर असातत्य होती है
opts.C: फलन की ऊपरी और निचली दोनों सीमाओं पर असातत्य होता है
opts.D: असातत्य हमेशा उच्च सीमा पर होता है

qs.sol: द्वितीय प्रकार के अनुचित समाकलन में असातत्य किसी भी सिरे या भीतर हो सकता है; यह हमेशा ऊपरी सीमा पर नहीं होता।
qs.rel: Concept: Type II improper integral has an unbounded integrand at an endpoint or interior point. Next: split at the singularity; p-test for 1/x^p on (0,1) needs p < 1.

qs.stem: रीमान समाकलनीय होने के लिए फलन के लिए, घात श्रेणी को प्रभावित करने की दशा में क्या स्थिति होगी?

opts.A: निम्न समाकलन उच्च समाकलन के समान है
opts.D: निम्न समाकलन उच्च समाकलन से कम है

qs.sol: डार्बू समाकलनीयता निचले और ऊपरी समाकलनों की समानता के तुल्य है।
qs.rel: Concept: Darboux integrability means lower integral equals upper integral. Next: equivalent epsilon criterion; Riemann sums converge; Lebesgue criterion with measure-zero discontinuities.

qs.stem: कौन सा रीमान समाकलन का गुण नहीं है?
qs.sol: रैखिकता, एकदिष्टता और अंतराल योज्यता रीमान समाकल के मानक गुण हैं।
qs.rel: Concept: Riemann integral properties: linearity, monotonicity, additivity over intervals. Next: |integral f| <= integral |f|; mean value theorem for integrals; reversal of limits changes sign.

qs.stem: प्रत्येक बंद (क्लोज़्ड) परिबद्ध अंतराल पर प्रत्येक सतत वास्तविक-मूल्यवान फलन _______ होता है।
qs.sol: बंद परिबद्ध अंतराल पर सतत वास्तविक फलन रीमान समाकलनीय होता है।
qs.rel: Concept: every continuous function on a closed bounded interval is Riemann integrable. Next: Heine-Borel compactness; boundedness; uniform continuity.

qs.stem: यदि किसी निश्चित समाकलन की सीमा अनंत है या समाकलन की सीमा के भीतर कहीं भी समाकल्य अनंत है, तो समाकलन को _________ कहा जाता है।
qs.sol: अनंत सीमा या अपरिबद्ध समाकल्य होने पर समाकल अनुचित होता है।
qs.rel: Concept: an integral with an infinite limit or unbounded integrand is improper. Next: Type I vs Type II; p-test: integral_1^infinity dx/x^p converges iff p > 1; comparison test.

qs.stem: अनुचित समाकल का मान ज्ञात करें ∫₀^∞ e^(-x) dx
qs.sol: −e^(−x) का मान सीमाओं पर रखने से 1 मिलता है।
qs.rel: Concept: improper integral of e^(-x) from 0 to infinity equals 1. Next: integral of e^(-ax) = 1/a; Gamma function value 1; integral of 1/x^2 from 1 to infinity = 1.

qs.stem: परिबद्ध फलन f:(a,b) →R रीमान समाकल है यदि और के वल यदि प्रत्येक Є> 0 के लिए एक विभाजन P [a,b] मौजूद है जो Є पर निर्भर हो सकता है, इस तरह कि ______________।
qs.sol: ऊपरी और निचले योगों का अंतर मनमाना छोटा हो सकता है।
qs.rel: Concept: epsilon-criterion for Riemann integrability: partition with U - L < epsilon. Next: Darboux upper and lower integrals equal; refinement lowers U - L; Riemann sums.

qs.stem: ℝ² में मूल बिंदु पर के न्द्रित त्रिज्या r की ओपन डिस्क D(x, y) का प्रतिनिधित्व क्या है?
qs.sol: मूलबिंदु से दूरी √(x²+y²) है; खुले डिस्क के भीतर होने की शर्त x²+y² < r² है।
qs.rel: Concept: open disc in R^2 is x^2 + y^2 < r^2. Next: closed disc uses <=; open ball in a metric space; unit ball in taxicab metric is a diamond.

qs.stem: Limit point of set {1/3, 4/11, 3/8, 8/21, …} is -
qs.sol:
Write the listed fractions as 2n/(5n+1) for n=1,2,3,4: 2/6, 4/11, 6/16, 8/21.

Dividing numerator and denominator by n gives 2/(5+1/n), which tends to 2/5.

qs.stem: The series ∑ₙ₌₁∞ nxe⁻ⁿˣ², ∀x ∈ R is -
qs.sol:
Modified from the official paper: “convergent” is narrowed to “convergent only for x ≠ 0” to remove a second true choice.

For fixed x≠0, r=e⁻ˣ²<1, so ∑nxe⁻ⁿˣ²=xr/(1−r)²; at x=0 every term is zero.

Uniform convergence would require the terms nxe⁻ⁿˣ² to tend uniformly to zero.

Taking x=1/√n gives √n/e, which does not tend to zero; convergence on R is non-uniform.

qs.stem: If A and B are non-empty bounded subsets of R and A+B = {x+y : x∈A, y∈B} and A−B = {x−y : x∈A, y∈B}, then incorrect statement is -
qs.sol:
For sums, suprema and infima add.

For differences, maximizing x−y uses the largest x and smallest y, so Sup(A−B)=Sup(A)−Inf(B), not subtraction of the upper bounds.

Minimizing uses Inf(A)−Sup(B).

qs.stem: If S₁ = ∫_{e²}^{e³} (log x)⁻² dx, and S₂ = ∫₂³ (eˣ/x²) dx, then -
qs.sol:
Set t = log x in S₁.

Then x = eᵗ, dx = eᵗdt, and the bounds become 2 and 3.

Thus S₁ = ∫₂³ eᵗ/t² dt = S₂.

qs.stem: Which of the following subsets of R² is convex set?
qs.sol:
The function x↦x² is convex; its epigraph {(x,y): y≥x²} is convex.

For two points above the parabola, Jensen’s inequality keeps every connecting segment above it.

qs.stem: If a function f(z) is continuous at point z = z₀, then which of the following statement is false?

opts.A: f(z) is continuous at z₀ for any path.
opts.B: f(z) is always analytic function at z₀.

qs.sol:
Continuity says the full complex limit exists and equals f(z₀).

Analyticity requires complex differentiability in a neighbourhood, which continuity alone cannot establish; f(z)=conjugate(z) is a counterexample.

qs.stem: Which of the following statement is false?

opts.A: The union of any arbitrary family of open sets is open.
opts.B: Every open interval is a nhd of each of its points.
opts.C: The intersection of a finite number of open sets is open.
opts.D: The set {1/n : n ∈ N} is open set.

qs.sol:
In the usual topology on R, arbitrary unions and finite intersections of open sets are open. Every point of an open interval has a small interval around it.

But each 1/n has nearby real numbers not in the listed reciprocal set, so that set is not open.

qs.stem: If Aₙ = [1/n, 1] ∀n ∈ N is an infinite closed set, then ⋃ₙ₌₁^∞ Aₙ is -
qs.sol:
Each set contains 1.

For any t strictly between 0 and 1, choose n≥1/t; then t∈[1/n,1].

Zero belongs to no member, so the union is (0,1].

qs.stem: Let f be a function defined on the interval [0, 1] as f(x) = {0, if x is rational; 1, if x is irrational}. Then f is -

opts.C: May or may not be R – integrable on [0, 1]

qs.sol:
Every subinterval of [0,1] contains rational and irrational numbers.

Therefore its infimum is 0 and supremum is 1.

Every lower Darboux sum is 0 and every upper sum is 1, so the two limits differ and the function is not Riemann integrable.

qs.stem: If f is a bounded function and p* is a refinement of a partition p then which of the following statement is true?
qs.sol:
Refining a partition replaces each interval by smaller subintervals.

The sum of subinterval infima cannot be lower than the old lower sum, so L(f,p*)≥L(f,p).

topics.deep:
- **Darboux sums:** for bounded f on [a,b] and partition P: L(f,P) = sum m_i delta x_i (m_i = inf f on subinterval) and U(f,P) = sum M_i delta x_i (M_i = sup). Lower integral = sup of L over all P; upper integral = inf of U. Always L(f,P) <= L(f,Q) <= U(f,Q) <= U(f,P) when Q refines P (P is contained in Q); and every lower sum <= every upper sum.
- **Riemann integrability criteria (equivalent):** (a) lower integral = upper integral; (b) for every epsilon > 0 there is a partition P with U(f,P) - L(f,P) < epsilon; (c) Riemann sums converge as mesh -> 0; (d) Lebesgue's criterion: f bounded and its set of discontinuities has measure zero. The existence of upper and lower integrals needs only f bounded and a < b on [a,b].
- **What is integrable:** continuous functions on [a,b]; monotone functions; bounded functions with finitely many discontinuities; products, sums, absolute values of integrable functions. Integrable does not imply continuous or differentiable. Every continuous real function on [a,b] is bounded (extreme value theorem) and integrable. Not integrable: Dirichlet's function (1 on Q, 0 on irrationals; every L = 0, every U = 1); unbounded functions.
- **Thomae's (popcorn) function:** f(p/q) = 1/q in lowest terms, 0 on irrationals. Continuous at irrationals, discontinuous at rationals, integrable with integral 0 because every lower sum is 0 and upper sums can be made small.
- **Properties:** linearity, monotonicity (f <= g implies integral f <= integral g), additivity (integral_a^c = integral_a^b + integral_b^c), |integral f| <= integral |f|, mean value theorem for integrals. Associativity is not named as an integral property. Fundamental theorem of calculus: F(x) = integral_a^x f is differentiable with F' = f at points of continuity; integral_a^b f = F(b) - F(a) for an antiderivative F.
- **Improper integrals:** Type I (infinite limit): integral_a^infinity f = lim_{b -> infinity} integral_a^b f. Type II (unbounded integrand at an endpoint or interior point): split at the singularity. p-tests: integral_1^infinity dx/x^p converges iff p > 1; integral_0^1 dx/x^p converges iff p < 1. integral_0^infinity e^(-x) dx = 1. Comparison test: 0 <= f <= g with g convergent implies f convergent. A Type II singularity can be at either end or inside the interval, not always the upper limit. Absolutely convergent improper Riemann integrals coincide with the Lebesgue integral; conditionally convergent ones (e.g. sin x/x over (0, infinity)) are not Lebesgue integrable.
- **Metric space axioms:** d(x,y) >= 0 with equality iff x = y; d(x,y) = d(y,x); d(x,z) <= d(x,y) + d(y,z). R^n has Euclidean d2, taxicab d1 = sum |xi - yi|, and max-metric d_infinity. Open ball B(x, r) = {y : d(x,y) < r}; the open disc in R^2 centred at the origin is {(x,y): x^2 + y^2 < r^2}.
- **Open and closed sets:** U is open if every point has a ball inside U. Unions of open sets are open, finite intersections are open. Closed = complement of open = contains all limit points. A set can be both (R, empty set), or neither ([0,1)). The closure of a set is the smallest closed superset. Interior = largest open subset. Boundary = closure minus interior.
- **Open set tests via continuity:** if g is continuous, then {g > c} and {g < c} are open and {g >= c} is closed. U = {(x,y): y > 0, x/y > 7} is the intersection of two such sets, so open; {(x,y): y/sin(x^2 y^3) > 2}, defined where the sine is non-zero, is open in the same way. Remember to write the domain restriction.
- **Continuity in metric spaces:** f is continuous at x iff for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(x,y) < delta implies d'(f(x), f(y)) < epsilon; equivalently f(B(x, delta)) is contained in B(f(x), epsilon). Global characterisation: f is continuous iff the pre-image of every open set is open (iff of every closed set is closed). A function continuous on a subset B is continuous at every point of B.
- **Topological invariants:** the continuous image of a connected set is connected; of a compact set is compact. In R^n, compact = closed and bounded (Heine-Borel). A continuous function on a compact set is bounded, attains max and min, and is uniformly continuous. Intermediate value theorem on [a,b].
- **Sequences and completeness:** convergent sequences are Cauchy; R^n and C[a,b] with sup-metric are complete; Q is not complete. Monotone bounded sequences converge. Bolzano-Weierstrass: every bounded sequence in R^n has a convergent subsequence.
- **Common traps:** assuming continuity implies differentiability; forgetting that the Riemann integral requires boundedness; calling [0,1) closed; mixing up refinement direction (lower sums increase, upper sums decrease when refining); claiming the Dirichlet function is integrable.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) is {x: x > 0} open or closed in R; (2) integral_1^infinity dx/x^2 and integral_0^1 dx/sqrt x; (3) convergence of integral_1^infinity dx/x; (4) which function is Riemann integrable among Dirichlet, Thomae, step; (5) condition for L(f,P) <= U(f,P); (6) definition of limit point; (7) is the unit circle compact; (8) can a continuous function map a connected set to a disconnected one; (9) verify metric axioms for a given d; (10) closure of the open interval (0,1) in R.

topics.title: Numerical Methods
topics.theory:
- **Runge-Kutta methods** solve **ordinary differential equations** (initial value problems) numerically. RK4: y_{n+1} = y_n + (h/6)(k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4).
- **Lagrange interpolation (2 points):** p(x) = y0 (x - x1)/(x0 - x1) + y1 (x - x0)/(x1 - x0). Through (2,3),(4,5): p(x) = x + 1. f(3) from (1,4),(5,6) = 5.
- **Linear interpolation** between two table points = line through them: y(5) from (2,8),(6,12) is 11.
- **Errors:** absolute error = |true - approx|; relative = abs. error / |true|; percentage error = relative x 100. Pi approx 22/7: abs error 0.0012645, rel 0.000402.
- **Truncation error** comes from replacing a function by a finite approximation (e.g. an interpolating polynomial, Taylor truncation); **round-off error** from limited digits.
- **Significant digits:** leading zeros are not significant. 0.000023 has 2 significant digits.
- **Backward difference (Newton):** y(x) = y_n + p grad y_n + p(p+1)/2! grad^2 y_n + ... with p = (x - x_n)/h.
- **Numerical differentiation (backward 2nd-order):** f'(x_n) ~ [3f(x_n) - 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_{n-2})]/(2h); forward: [-3f0 + 4f1 - f2]/(2h); central: [f(x+h) - f(x-h)]/(2h).
- **Newton-Raphson:** x_{n+1} = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n), quadratic convergence. **Bisection:** linear. 
- **Trapezoidal rule** h/2[y0 + 2(y1+...+y_{n-1}) + yn]; **Simpson 1/3** h/3[y0 + 4(odd) + 2(even) + yn] (n even).
- **Euler method:** y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n); local error O(h^2), global O(h).
- **Derivative from a table:** pick the formula that matches the position of the point (forward at start, backward at end, central inside).

qs.stem: Runge–Kutta method is used for _____.

opts.D: Solution of system of linear equation

qs.sol:
The Runge-Kutta method is a powerful family of iterative techniques used for the numerical approximation of solutions to differential equations.

Explanation of the Method
The primary purpose of the Runge-Kutta method is to solve ordinary differential equations (ODEs), particularly initial value problems. Instead of seeking an analytical (exact) solution, which may be difficult or impossible to find for complex equations, the Runge-Kutta method approximates the solution by taking small, calculated steps along the function's curve. …
qs.rel: Concept: Runge-Kutta solves ordinary differential equations (initial value problems). Next: RK4 weights 1, 2, 2, 1 over 6; Euler order 1; Simpson/trapezoid are for integration.

qs.stem: If f(1) = 4 and f(5) = 6, then what is the value of f(3) using Lagrange’s interpolation?
qs.sol:
Using the two-point Lagrange interpolation formula for (1, 4) and (5, 6):

f(3) = 4 * (3 - 5)/(1 - 5) + 6 * (3 - 1)/(5 - 1)
     = 4 * (1/2) + 6 * (1/2)
     = 2 + 3
     = 5.

Therefore, f(3) = 5.
qs.rel: Concept: two-point Lagrange interpolation (a straight line). Next: three-point Lagrange gives a quadratic; linear interpolation error; Newton divided differences give the same polynomial.

qs.stem:
What is Lagrange’s interpolation polynomial for the following data?

Data shown: x = 2, 4; f(x) = 3, 5.
qs.sol: The displayed data points are (2,3) and (4,5). The degree-one Lagrange interpolant has slope (5−3)/(4−2)=1 and intercept 3−2=1, hence p(x)=x+1.
qs.rel: Concept: Lagrange polynomial through two points (slope 1, intercept 1). Next: through three points degree <= 2; uniqueness of interpolating polynomial; evaluate at an interior x.

qs.stem: Which of the following errors is caused by replacing a tabulated function by means of an interpolating polynomial in numerical computation of derivatives?
qs.sol:
An interpolating polynomial approximates the original tabulated function.

The discarded interpolation terms cause truncation error in the derivative.
qs.rel: Concept: replacing a function by an interpolating polynomial causes truncation error. Next: round-off error from finite digits; inherent error; differentiation magnifies errors.

qs.stem: An approximation value of Π is given by X1 = 22/7 = 3.1428571 and its true value X = 3.1415926. Find the absolute and relative errors, respectively.
qs.sol: X − X1 = 3.1415926 − 3.1428571 = −0.0012645. The signed relative error (X − X1)/X ≈ −0.000402503. True absolute error is |X − X1| = 0.0012645, and absolute relative error is |X − X1|/|X| ≈ 0.000402503. The printed question asks for “absolute” errors, but the official key uses signed values and truncates the relative result to −0.000402; the keyed answer is retained.
qs.rel: Concept: absolute and relative error, pi vs 22/7. Next: percentage error = relative x 100; significant digits; true error signed vs absolute.

qs.stem: The digits that are used to express a number is called ______ and the number 0.000023 contains ______.
qs.sol:
Significant digits convey the meaningful precision of a number.

Leading zeros are placeholders, so 0.000023 has only the digits 2 and 3 significant.
qs.rel: Concept: significant digits (leading zeros do not count). Next: 0.000023 has 2 significant digits; rounding to n digits; trailing zeros after a decimal count.

qs.stem: If x = 5, then what is the value of y from the following table of values?
qs.sol:
The table provides two points: (2, 8) and (6, 12).

Calculate the slope (m): m = (12 - 8) / (6 - 2) = 4 / 4 = 1.

Find the y-intercept (b) using the equation y = mx + b: 8 = 1(2) + b, so b = 6.

The linear equation is: y = x + 6.

Substitute x = 5 into the equation: y = 5 + 6 = 11.

Final Answer: Option 3 (11)

qs.stem: If α₁, α₂ are roots of the equation x² + px + q = 0, then iteration xₙ₊₁ = −q/(xₙ + p) will converge near root x = α₁, if -
qs.sol:
For g(x) = −q/(x+p), local convergence at α₁ requires |g′(α₁)| < 1.

Since q = α₁α₂ and α₁+p = −α₂, |g′(α₁)| = |α₁/α₂|.

Thus the first root must have smaller modulus.

qs.stem: With usual notation, for y(20) = 24, y(24) = 32, y(28) = 35 and y(32) = 40, approximate value of y(25) by Bessel’s interpolation formula is -

Use Bessel interpolation about x=24 and 28: h=4 and u=(25−24)/4=1/4.

The central first difference is 35−32=3; the mean second difference is (−5+2)/2=−1.5, and the third difference is 7.

Thus y(25)=32+u(3)+u(u−1)(−1.5)/2+(u−1/2)u(u−1)(7)/6=32.9453125.

This rounds to 32.9 to one decimal place; 32.8 is the nearest offered value.

qs.sol:
Simpson’s one-third rule fits a quadratic interpolant y=ax²+bx+c through each three consecutive ordinates.

Such parabolas have vertical axes, that is, axes parallel to the y-axis.

qs.stem: The Newton’s divided difference polynomial, which satisfies the data f(0) = 1, f(1) = 3, f(3) = 55, is -
qs.sol:
Write f(x)=ax²+bx+c. From f(0)=1, c=1; f(1)=3 gives a+b=2.

From f(3)=55, 9a+3b=54; solving gives a=8,b=−6. Thus f(x)=8x²−6x+1.

qs.stem: If Δf(x) = eᵃˣ⁺ᵇ, then f(0), Δf(0) and Δ²f(0) are -
qs.sol:
Note on the official key: The board keys “in geometric progression”; the given finite difference does not determine f(0), so the three values need not form a geometric progression. This question is graded by the official key.

For h=1, a=ln 2 and b=0, every f(x)=2ˣ+C has Δf(x)=2ˣ. Choosing C=1 gives f(0), Δf(0), Δ²f(0) as 2, 1, 1.

qs.stem: The order of convergence of Newton-Raphson method is -
qs.sol:
For a simple root α with f′(α)≠0, Taylor expansion of the Newton update gives eₙ₊₁≈[f″(α)/(2f′(α))]eₙ².

The leading error is proportional to the square of the previous error, giving order two.

qs.stem: The value of (Δ−∇)x², where h is the interval of difference, (Δ, ∇ are usual notations), is -
qs.sol:
The forward difference is Δx²=(x+h)²−x²=2xh+h².

The backward difference is ∇x²=x²−(x−h)²=2xh−h². Their difference is 2h².

qs.stem: Modified from the official paper: Which closed Newton–Cotes rule uses two equal subintervals and the formula I ≈ (h/3)(y₀ + 4y₁ + y₂)?
qs.sol:
Modified from the official paper: its printed formula has binomial weights and gives 2h(y₀+2y₁+y₂) at n=2, so the formula was corrected.

With two equal subintervals, the closed three-ordinate rule weights the endpoint and midpoint values 1:4:1.

Substitution gives I ≈ (h/3)(y₀+4y₁+y₂), which is Simpson’s one-third rule.

qs.stem: Given – x: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4; y: 4, 8, 15, 7, 6; for the polynomial of degree at most four interpolating these values, the value of dy/dx at x = 0 will be equal to –
qs.sol:
Modified from the official paper: the printed table does not determine an arbitrary derivative; take the unique degree-at-most-four interpolating polynomial.

At spacing h=1 its first forward differences are Δy₀=4, Δ²y₀=3, Δ³y₀=−18, Δ⁴y₀=40.

Newton forward differentiation at x=0 gives y′(0)=Δy₀−Δ²y₀/2+Δ³y₀/3−Δ⁴y₀/4.

Substitution yields 4−3/2−18/3−40/4=−13.5.

qs.stem: Interpolation formulae are based on the fundamental assumption that the data can be expressed as –
qs.sol:
An interpolating polynomial is constructed through the given data points.

Linear and quadratic interpolants are only low-degree special cases.

The general finite-difference and Lagrange formulas assume polynomial representation.

qs.stem: Which interpolation formula does not have any difference operator?
qs.sol:
Lagrange interpolation forms a sum of products of (x−xⱼ)/(xᵢ−xⱼ) times observed values.

It uses node coordinates directly, with no finite-difference operator.

The other listed formulas are difference-table formulas.

qs.stem: The method for determination of a root of a non – linear equation which uses two initial guess roots but does not require that they must bracket the root, is?
qs.sol:
The secant iteration uses two earlier approximations to construct a secant line.

Its zero gives the next approximation; a sign-changing bracket is unnecessary.

topics.deep:
- **Errors:** true value x, approximation x1. Absolute error = |x - x1|; relative error = |x - x1|/|x|; percentage error = 100 x relative. Example: pi vs 22/7: x - x1 = 3.1415926 - 3.1428571 = -0.0012645, so absolute error 0.0012645 and relative error 0.0012645/3.1415926 = 0.0004025 (0.04 percent). Sources: inherent, round-off (finite digits), truncation (series or formula cut off), and discretisation. Truncation error arises when a function is replaced by an interpolating polynomial or Taylor polynomial.
- **Significant digits:** all non-zero digits, zeros between non-zero digits, and trailing zeros after a decimal point count; leading zeros do not. 0.000023 has 2 significant digits; 1200.0 has 5; 0.0305 has 3. Rounding to n significant digits gives a relative error <= 5 x 10^-n.
- **Finite differences:** forward Delta y_i = y_(i+1) - y_i; backward Nabla y_i = y_i - y_(i-1); central delta. For polynomial of degree k, the k-th differences are constant and the (k+1)-th are zero. Table check: y = x^2 + 1 at x = 0,1,2,3 gives 1, 2, 5, 10; first differences 1, 3, 5; second differences 2, 2.
- **Newton's forward formula:** y(x) = y0 + p Delta y0 + p(p-1)/2! Delta^2 y0 + p(p-1)(p-2)/3! Delta^3 y0 + ..., with p = (x - x0)/h. Use near the start of the table. Example: y(1.5) with the table above, p = 1.5: 1 + 1.5(1) + (1.5)(0.5)/2 (2) = 3.25. **Newton's backward formula:** y(x) = y_n + p Nabla y_n + p(p+1)/2! Nabla^2 y_n + ..., p = (x - x_n)/h (negative), use near the end.
- **Lagrange interpolation (unequal spacing):** P(x) = sum y_i L_i(x), with L_i(x) = product_{j != i} (x - x_j)/(x_i - x_j). Two points: P(x) = y0 (x - x1)/(x0 - x1) + y1 (x - x0)/(x1 - x0), a straight line. For (2,3), (4,5): P(x) = x + 1. For (1,4), (5,6) at x = 3: 4(1/2) + 6(1/2) = 5. The Lagrange polynomial through n+1 points has degree <= n and is unique. Error: f(x) - P(x) = f^(n+1)(xi) / (n+1)! x product (x - x_i).
- **Divided differences (Newton):** f[x0,x1] = (f1 - f0)/(x1 - x0); P(x) = f0 + (x - x0) f[x0,x1] + (x - x0)(x - x1) f[x0,x1,x2] + ...; symmetric in the nodes.
- **Linear interpolation from a table:** (2,8), (6,12): slope 1, y = x + 6, so y(5) = 11. Extrapolation is risky.
- **Numerical differentiation:** forward f'(x0) ~ (f1 - f0)/h (error O(h)); backward (f_n - f_(n-1))/h; central (f(x+h) - f(x-h))/(2h) with error O(h^2); three-point forward (-3f0 + 4f1 - f2)/(2h); three-point backward (3f_n - 4f_(n-1) + f_(n-2))/(2h). Table with f(4) = 35, f(3) = 27, f(2) = 22 and h = 1: f'(4) ~ (105 - 108 + 22)/2 = 9.5. Differentiation by differences magnifies errors; the error from replacing a function by an interpolating polynomial is truncation error.
- **Numerical integration:** trapezoidal rule (h/2)[y0 + 2(y1 + ... + y_(n-1)) + y_n], error O(h^2). Simpson's 1/3 rule (h/3)[y0 + 4(y1 + y3 + ...) + 2(y2 + y4 + ...) + y_n], n even, error O(h^4), exact for cubics. Simpson's 3/8 needs n multiple of 3. Example: integral_0^1 x^2 dx with n = 2: trapezoid 0.375, Simpson 1/3 exact.
- **Root finding:** bisection (always converges, linear, halves the interval); regula falsi; **Newton-Raphson** x_(n+1) = x_n - f(x_n)/f'(x_n), quadratic convergence, fails if f' = 0; secant method order 1.618. Example: f = x^2 - 2, x0 = 1: x1 = 1.5, x2 = 1.41667, x3 = 1.41422. Fixed-point iteration x = g(x) converges if |g'| < 1. Gauss elimination, Gauss-Jordan, Gauss-Seidel (needs diagonal dominance) for linear systems.
- **ODE solvers:** Euler y_(n+1) = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n), local error O(h^2), global O(h). Modified Euler/Heun and RK2 are second order. **RK4:** k1 = h f(x,y); k2 = h f(x + h/2, y + k1/2); k3 = h f(x + h/2, y + k2/2); k4 = h f(x + h, y + k3); y_new = y + (k1 + 2k2 + 2k3 + k4)/6, global error O(h^4). Runge-Kutta methods are used for **ordinary differential equations** (initial-value problems), not for integration of tables or linear systems. Example: y' = x + y, y(0) = 1, h = 0.1: k1 = 0.1, k2 = 0.11, k3 = 0.1105, k4 = 0.12105; y(0.1) = 1 + 0.66205/6 = 1.11034 (exact 1.11034).
- **Common traps:** using the forward formula at the end of a table; confusing absolute and relative error; counting leading zeros as significant; equating RK4 with an integration formula; forgetting that sign of the signed error is negative when the approximation is larger than the true value.
- **Likely question angles:** (1) build a difference table and find the missing value; (2) y(x) at an interior point by Newton forward; (3) one step of Euler for y' = x + y; (4) number of significant digits in 0.00340; (5) relative error in approximating sqrt2 by 1.41; (6) two Newton-Raphson iterations for sqrt of 5; (7) order of convergence of bisection/Newton; (8) Simpson 1/3 for integral_0^2 x^3 dx with n = 4; (9) central difference derivative estimate from a table; (10) which method suits a stiff or initial-value ODE problem.
